posts.title: Why a weekly file scan stalled over the VPN, and how the fix brought it to 24 minutes
posts.summary: A root cause analysis of a compliance scan that ran at about 178 items per second on the office LAN and about 7 over the VPN, and the four changes that made it reliable.

body.p: FileGate audits every item on the agency file share against the naming and records policy once a week, about 67,000 files and folders. The scan worked in testing, then stalled in production.

The first step was a benchmark, not a code change. The same scan ran against the same share from two places: on the office LAN and over the WireGuard VPN. On the LAN it processed about **178 items per second**. Over the VPN it processed about **7**, roughly 25 times slower. At that rate the directory walk alone takes hours, and a dropped connection could cost the entire run.

The code wasn't slow; the network path was. A scan like this is dominated by small metadata operations: list a folder, read a name, check a timestamp. Each one is a network round trip, so extra latency is multiplied by every item in the tree. Bandwidth barely matters when no single request moves much data.

ul: **A network gate.** The scan now checks that it is on the office network before it starts, and refuses to run over the VPN instead of limping along.
**Incremental commits.** Results are written in batches as the scan goes, so an interruption loses minutes of work instead of the whole run.
**Explicit failure states.** A run ends as completed, failed or interrupted, with the reason recorded. "Still running" is no longer a state that can last forever.
**The right host.** The weekly job moved to an always-on machine on the office network, so nobody's laptop has to stay awake and connected.

body.p: The production scan on September 22, 2026 processed **67,240 items in 24 minutes with 0 errors**. The benchmark also changed a broader decision: bulk file workloads now run on-network by default, and the VPN is for people, not batch jobs.

ul: Benchmark the same workload on both paths before touching code. The ratio tells you whether you have a software problem or a placement problem.
Metadata-heavy jobs are latency-bound. Move the job to the data rather than the data to the job.
Long-running jobs need checkpoints and a defined way to fail.

body.p: The policy rule engine is available as a standalone open-source tool: [naming-policy-validator](https://github.com/forrestswan3/naming-policy-validator).

posts.title: Windows silently drops trailing periods from folder names, and your naming policy should know
posts.summary: A naming-policy test passed on Linux and failed on Windows because "Sample Bakery, LLC." quietly became "Sample Bakery, LLC". Here is why, and how to write rules that survive it.

body.p: Our records policy names business client folders with the legal suffix, as in `Sample Bakery, LLC.`, with a period after the suffix. When I published a clean-room version of the policy engine, the end-to-end test built a sample folder tree and audited it. It passed on Linux. On the Windows CI runner the same test failed: a business folder that should have been compliant was flagged.

The folder was never created with the period. Windows path normalization trims trailing periods and spaces from the last segment of a path, so a request to create `Sample Bakery, LLC.` produces `Sample Bakery, LLC`. No error, no warning. Microsoft's own naming guidance says not to end a file or folder name with a space or a period, because even where the file system can store one, the Windows shell and user interface don't support it.

Prefixing a path with `\\?\` skips normalization and can create the name as typed, but then staff get a folder that Explorer and many applications can't open or rename properly. That trades one problem for a worse one.

body.h: Why it matters beyond a test

body.p: If your file server stores names created from a non-Windows system, or a policy demands a trailing period, people on Windows will either be unable to create compliant names or will end up with names that behave strangely. A compliance scan will then flag work that staff physically couldn't do right.

ul: Make the period after a business suffix optional in the policy pattern: `(?:LLC|Inc|Corp|LLP|PLLC)\.?`.
Add a note to the written policy so humans and code agree.
Run the test suite on Windows as well as Linux, because the operating system your users run is part of the specification.

body.p: A naming standard is only valid if it can be followed on the platforms people actually use. Test naming rules where the files get created, not just where the code runs.

References: Microsoft, [Naming files, paths, and namespaces](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file). The validator with the Windows-safe example policy: [naming-policy-validator](https://github.com/forrestswan3/naming-policy-validator).

posts.title: Rolling out WireGuard to 20+ Windows users without giving anyone admin rights
posts.summary: WireGuard for Windows normally needs Administrator rights to manage tunnels. Its limited operator UI lets standard users connect and disconnect without ever seeing a key.

body.p: When the agency moved to a pfSense firewall with a WireGuard VPN, the plan hit a familiar wall. WireGuard for Windows expects an administrator to manage tunnels, and the team's laptops run as standard users. The usual outcomes are both bad: hand out local admin rights, or have IT take a ticket every time someone needs to connect.

WireGuard for Windows has a documented, easy-to-miss option called the limited operator UI. With it turned on, members of the built-in Windows **Network Configuration Operators** group can start and stop tunnels from the WireGuard window. Their view has keys stripped, and they can't add, edit, import, export or delete configurations.

ul: Copy the device's own configuration into a folder only Administrators and SYSTEM can read.
Install the tunnel as a Windows service with `wireguard.exe /installtunnelservice`.
Add the user to Network Configuration Operators, then have them sign out and back in once.
Delete the original configuration file, since it contains the private key.
Use one key pair per device. Don't reuse a configuration across people or machines, and don't send configurations or keys by email or chat.
Prefer split tunneling, so only office networks go through the tunnel, unless you mean to route all traffic.
Revoke on the server. Removing the peer on the firewall belongs in the offboarding checklist, because deleting the app from a laptop doesn't revoke anything.

ol: Did a handshake happen recently? If not, look at the endpoint, the keys, or whether the server lists this peer.
Is the target reachable? A handshake with no traffic points at allowed IPs, routing, NAT or firewall rules on the server side.

body.p: More than 20 remote and in-office users connect on their own, nobody received local admin rights for it, and access is revoked in one place when someone leaves.

The scripts are open source: [wireguard-nonadmin-windows](https://github.com/forrestswan3/wireguard-nonadmin-windows). Reference: WireGuard for Windows [enterprise usage documentation](https://git.zx2c4.com/wireguard-windows/about/docs/enterprise.md).
